definition: In natural language processing, linguistics, and neighboring fields, Linguistic Linked Open Data (LLOD) describes a method and an interdisciplinary community concerned with creating, sharing, and (re-)using language resources in accordance with Linked Data principles.
details: The Linguistic Linked Open Data Cloud was conceived and is maintained by the Open Linguistics Working Group (OWLG) of the Open Knowledge Foundation, but has been a point of focal activity for several W3C community groups, research projects, and infrastructure efforts since then.

explainer.lead: LLOD is a method and interdisciplinary community for creating, sharing, and reusing language resources under Linked Data principles. It matters because it lets language datasets interconnect and be reused across projects instead of sitting in isolated silos.

tiers.eli5: It is like giving every language dataset a web address and linking them together, so tools can follow the links from one resource to another the way you follow links on a website.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers publish and consume language resources as linked, resolvable data so lexicons, corpora, and annotations can be combined across sources. The pitfall is that reuse depends on shared vocabularies and stable identifiers, which many resources do not consistently provide.
tiers.paperLevel: Resources are expressed according to Linked Data principles, meaning they are identified and connected so they can be shared and (re-)used; the LLOD Cloud is maintained by the Open Linguistics Working Group of the Open Knowledge Foundation and has been a focus of W3C community groups and infrastructure efforts.

explainer.example: A lexicon and an annotated corpus are published with shared identifiers, letting a query pull a word's entry and its corpus occurrences together.
